summary:
The Cook Islands removed the male-sex offences from its Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. Sections 154 and 155 of the Crimes Act 1969 had criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent explicitly not a defence. Reporting on the repeal describes the offences as never enforced. Reported maximum terms differ: 2017 coverage gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while 2023 reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to 10 years.

The repeal followed a repeatedly deferred reform path. A 2017 draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help and intended to replace the 1969 Crimes Act, would have removed sections 154 and 155. A select committee recommended removal, and sodomy and “indecent acts between men” were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked. In October 2020 MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. The note attached to the 2023 amendment cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands.

Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000. A trans visitor in a relationship that local authorities would class as same-sex has no access to marriage recognition.

The 2023 amendment also added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting traces the criminal provisions to colonial-era law and states that colonisation introduced the taboo into a society described as historically accepting.

The victim-protection provisions added in 2023 are not specific to LGBT people and do not create trans-specific safeguards.
localsOnly:
The Cook Islands has a population of 21,000. The Te Tiare Association is the country's only LGBTI community group; it welcomed the 2017 draft repeal, and member Valentino Wichman was quoted on the law's homophobia.

Public submissions on the draft Crimes Bill opened in Parliament in August 2017. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed that a submission from the Te Tiare Association was already before the select committee, and at least three lawyers were expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address trans-specific document markers, bathroom or facilities access, hate-crime protections, or police treatment of trans visitors. No trans-specific violence data is provided.

The 2023 repeal concerns male same-sex offences and does not establish trans-specific protections. The reported maximum penalties for the repealed offences differ between the 2017 and 2023 sources; the discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.
